title: What is known about 1RB1LF_1LC0RD_---1LA_0LA0RE_1LA1RA_1LB0LD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LF_1LC0RD_---1LA_0LA0RE_1LA1RA_1LB0LD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to an orbit. The run is a sequence of rounds; a round takes D> 0 0 111 0 1^n T to D> 0 0 111 0 1^n' T' with n' = 4⌊(n−1)/3⌋ + d, where (d, T') is computed from the tail T and (n−1) mod 3 alone. Lean proves this round map for every tail on which its simulator answers, and that, as long as it answers along the orbit, the machine halts from blank tape exactly when the orbit reaches a halting round. The map has been iterated for 2·106 rounds without a halt (and it always answered). A random-model estimate puts the chance of a halt near 10-15 per round: halting is expected eventually but only after an astronomically long run.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 39,843 cells have been visited and 29,918 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.501). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.079).

claims.title: The sweeps
claims.text: From A> 0 11 0 11 0 111 (0111)^k 0 1^(m+4) T at the left end, one sweep (10k + 45 steps) takes three ones from the block and adds a counting block 1110: (0111)^(k+1) 0 1^(m+1); by induction any number of sweeps.

claims.title: Rounds for the tails empty, 011 and 010111
claims.text: For n = c + 1 + 3t: from D> 0 0 111 0 1^n T the machine reaches the next round start D> 0 0 111 0 1^(4t+d) T', for all t, with (d, T') = (11, T) or (7, next tail) for T empty or 011 (c = 1 gives the 7), and (19, empty) for T = 010111 and c ≠ 1. The theorem round states it for the map next.

claims.title: The run from blank tape enters the rounds
claims.text: After 51 steps the tape is the round start D> 0 0 111 0 1^3 (n = 3, empty tail).

claims.title: Some round starts halt
claims.text: The round start with 57 ones and the tail 0110101010 11 (blocks of ones 2, 1, 1, 1, 2) halts within 2,575 steps. So the halting transition is reachable from the round shape; the question is whether the orbit from blank tape gets such a tail.

claims.title: The round map for every tail
claims.text: After the sweeps the tape is 0 11 0 11 0 111 (0111)^t 0 1^c T. A simulator keeps one copy of 0111 on each side, works cell by cell in the two ends, and crosses the t − 2 copies between only whole, by six shift rules; it never looks at t. Lean proves that whatever it answers is what the machine does: if roundMap (n, T) = (n', T') the machine goes from the round start (n, T) to the round start (n', T'), with n' = 4(t − 2) + N and (N, T') depending only on T and c; if it answers halt the machine halts in that round. For all n ≥ 7 and every word T. The simulator may also answer stuck (a meeting with the block that the six rules do not cover, or out of fuel); that has not been seen for any tail.

claims.title: Reduction to the orbit
claims.text: Let orbit be the orbit of the round map from (11, empty tail), the second round start of the run. If the map never answers stuck along the orbit, the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit reaches a halting round. Without any hypothesis: a halting round in the orbit gives a halt, and an orbit that goes on for ever gives a run that never halts.

claims.title: The first 500 rounds of the orbit
claims.text: Lean's kernel evaluates the round map along the orbit: it answers with a next round for each of the first 500 rounds (no halt, never stuck); after ten rounds the block has 579 ones and the tail is empty.

claims.title: The Lean round map agrees with plain simulation
claims.text: py/zonemap.py is the same simulator in Python. On the first 3,000 tails reachable from the empty tail with any c (about 7,900 cases) it gives the same answer as a plain simulation of the round with two values of t (py/roundmap.py), halting cases included, and it never answers stuck. The plain simulation agrees with the machine for the first 22 rounds (1.4·108 steps).

claims.title: Orbit: 2·10<sup>6</sup> rounds, no halt, never stuck
claims.text: Iterating the round map from (11, empty tail) for 2·10<sup>6</sup> rounds (n then has 249,880 decimal digits) never reaches a halting tail and the simulator always answers; only 26 tails occur (the empty tail and 011 in 78% of the rounds, each deeper level about three times rarer), the longest with five blocks of ones (2, 1, 2, 1, 3). The nearest halting tail, blocks 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, is 36 rounds from the empty tail, 29 of them pushes.

claims.title: Random model: halts eventually, but astronomically late
claims.text: If c is uniform and independent from round to round (it is, empirically, for each tail), the tail is a recurrent Markov chain that returns to empty with probability 1, and the chance that an excursion hits a halting tail is between about 10<sup>-18</sup> (one shortest path) and 10<sup>-13</sup> (no halting mass found with paths pruned below 10<sup>-13</sup>). So the model halts with probability 1, after some 10<sup>13</sup>–10<sup>18</sup> rounds; since n grows by 4/3 per round and a round takes about n<sup>2</sup>/3 steps, that is far beyond any simulation.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. By the reduction it halts iff the orbit of the round map reaches a halting (tail, c) pair (given that the map keeps answering, as it has for 2·10<sup>6</sup> rounds): a question about the base-3 digits of a number multiplied by about 4/3 each round, like other Collatz-like cryptids.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine runs in rounds: a block of ones is eaten three at a time and comes back 4/3 as long, while a short tail at the right end acts as a tiny stack driven by the block's length mod 3. Some tail shapes halt; the run has not produced one in 10<sup>6</sup> rounds.

facts.text: Sweeps and the round map for the three commonest tails, proved in Lean.
Orbit of the round map from blank tape: no halting tail.
Chance of a halt per round in a random model.

sections.heading: Rounds, sweeps and a tail
html: At the start of every round the whole tape is D> 0 0 111 0 1n T: the head at the left end in state D, a long block of n ones, and a short tail T on the right. During the round the head sweeps back and forth across the tape. Each sweep runs right to the block of ones, takes three ones from it and comes back, leaving one more counting block 1110 on the left; the tape grows by one cell on the left every sweep. That is why the left side grows like the square root of the step count.

When only 1, 2 or 3 ones are left (n = c + 1 + 3t, c ∈ {0, 1, 2}), the end of the round turns each of the t counting blocks (4 cells) back into four ones, works a little on the tail, and the next round starts with n' = 4t + d ones. The tape reaches one cell further to the right only at these ends, once per round, and rounds come exponentially further apart: the right side grows like the logarithm.

sections.heading: The round map, for every tail at once
html: The end of a round looks different for every tail, and there are infinitely many tails. What they share: after the sweeps the tape is 0 11 0 11 0 111 (0111)t 0 1c T, and the head only ever crosses the long run of counting blocks whole, in one of six ways (for example in state A, left to right, turning every 0111 into 1001). So the round end can be computed by a small simulator that keeps one counting block on each side, steps cell by cell at the two ends, and jumps over the t − 2 blocks between by a shift rule. It never looks at t.

Lean proves that whatever this simulator answers is what the machine does, for every t (lean/Zone.lean, generic; lean/Reduction.lean, this machine). The result is a computable round map roundMap (n, T) = (4(t − 2) + N, T'), halt, or stuck (no answer), and the theorem halts_iff: if the map never answers stuck along the orbit of (11, empty tail), the machine halts from blank tape exactly when that orbit reaches a halting round. The kernel checks the first 500 rounds; the same simulator in Python has run 2·106 rounds and agrees with plain simulation on about 7,900 (tail, c) cases.
What is still missing for a statement with no hypothesis is a proof that the simulator never gets stuck, i.e. a description of all reachable tails.

sections.heading: Where a halt could come from
html: The sweeps and the common round ends never halt. The tail behaves like a small stack: a round with c = 1 (probability about 1/3) pushes it one shape deeper, other rounds keep it or pop it back toward empty. Some deep shapes make the end of the round run into the halting transition (C reading 0): the shortest one found, with blocks of ones 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, needs 36 rounds in a row of the right kind (29 pushes). Lean checks that such a round start really halts.

In 106 rounds from blank tape the deepest tail had five blocks of ones; tails come up about three times less often for each step of depth. If the residues c behave like dice, a halt is certain eventually, but only after about 1013 to 1018 rounds, when n has more than 1012 digits. Deciding it means understanding the base-3 digits of an orbit of n → 4⌊(n−1)/3⌋ + d, which is out of reach, as for Antihydra.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.501). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.079).
After 109 steps the tape spans 39,843 cells (29,237 left of the start, 55 right), with a density of 1s of 0.751.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A 4/3 growth map on one block of ones (n -> 4·floor((n-1)/3) + const) with a stack-like 'tail' at the right end; Lean proves the round map for every tail (computed by a simulator that never looks at n) and the reduction to its orbit; some tails halt, the orbit has not met one in 2 million rounds.
